wstep: This card describes the NCHFP recipe for corncob jelly: a jelly made from the liquid of boiled red field corn cobs with powdered pectin and sugar, processed in a boiling-water bath.

sekcje.naglowek: Why you must follow the recipe exactly
akapity: Sweet corn has a pH of 7.3 according to an FDA table of approximate values.
NCHFP tested this recipe with SURE-JELL Premium Fruit Pectin and states that the recipe, as tested, produces an acidic jelly.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): JarAtlas has no data for sweet corn cobs or for other substitutions, so follow the recipe exactly, with red field corn cobs and without changing the amounts.
NCHFP warns not to reduce the sugar in traditional recipes: too little sugar prevents gelling and may allow yeasts and molds to grow.
NCHFP uses US measures: a cup holds about 237 ml.
For the corncob liquid NCHFP uses 12 (a dozen) medium-sized fresh red corncobs from field corn, cobs only, and 2 quarts (about 1.9 l) of water.
For the jelly: 3 cups of corncob liquid, 1 package (1 3/4 ounces) of powdered pectin and 3 cups of sugar; this makes about 4 half-pint jars.
Wash the corncobs and cut them into 4-inch (about 10 cm) lengths.
Put them in a large stockpot, add 2 quarts of water or enough to cover them, and bring to a boil.
Reduce the heat and boil slowly for 35 to 40 minutes.
Strain the liquid through a double layer of cheesecloth or a jelly bag and let it drip through; do not press or squeeze the bag or cloth.
Measure 3 cups of corncob liquid into a large saucepot; if needed, add water to make 3 cups.
Stir in the pectin and bring to a boil.
Add all the sugar at once and, stirring, bring the mixture back to a full rolling boil.
Boil for 5 minutes, remove from the heat and skim off the foam quickly.
JarAtlas uses the NCHFP option without pre-sterilizing the jars: wash and rinse the jars in hot water and keep them hot until filling; the processing time is then longer.
Pour the hot jelly immediately into the hot jars, leaving 1/4 inch (about 0.6 cm) of headspace.
Wipe the jar rims with a damp clean paper towel, put on two-piece metal lids and process in a boiling-water canner.
At 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) process half-pint and pint jars in a boiling-water bath for 10 minutes.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
At 1001–6000 ft (above 300 m up to 1800 m) process them for 15 minutes.
Above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) process them for 20 minutes.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
The NCHFP table gives times only for half-pint and pint jars.
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): a pint holds about 473 ml, so a 0.5 l jar has no tested time in this recipe; use jars of up to 473 ml.
Discard jelly with mold on it; USDA and microbiologists advise against scooping out the mold and eating the rest.
